section.title: Sequences
section.p: A sequence is a function whose inputs are whole numbers.

That sounds dry, but the idea is familiar. A table of decimal approximations is a sequence. The outputs of Newton’s method form a sequence. The yearly values in a population model form a sequence. The finite approximations to an integral form a sequence.
The input is not a continuous variable like x or t. It is a counting index:

statement.p: A sequence can also be given recursively. That means each term is built from earlier terms.
The rule does not give a_n directly. It gives instructions for producing the next term from the current one.
Recursive sequences are important because many algorithms work this way. Newton’s method, Euler’s method, and many population models produce a next value from a current value.

exercise.title: What does it mean for a sequence to converge?

statement.p: A sequence converges to L if its terms get arbitrarily close to L as n becomes large. In your own words, why is that stronger than saying the later terms look nearby in a table, and how is oscillating between two values different from growing without bound?

hint.p: Convergence is a promise about every required closeness, not a snapshot of a few terms. Oscillation refuses to choose one landing place; unbounded growth refuses to land at all.

paragraphs.title: A warning about sampling
paragraphs.p: A sequence is a list, not a continuous curve. Even when a formula involves a familiar continuous function, the sampled values may not settle.

exercise.title: Why can sampling a familiar formula fail to have a limit?

statement.p: The values a_n=\sin(n\pi/2) come from a continuous function, yet the sequence does not converge. In your own words, why is a sequence a list rather than a curve, and why can the sampled points refuse to settle even when the formula looks familiar?

hint.p: The index n jumps. What happens between integers is not part of the sequence, so a continuous picture can hide a jumping list.

exercise.title: Why do both monotonicity and boundedness matter?

statement.p: The Monotone Convergence Theorem says that an increasing sequence bounded above must converge, and likewise for a decreasing sequence bounded below. In your own words, why is monotone alone not enough, why is bounded alone not enough, and what completeness of the real line is doing in the argument?

hint.p: An increasing sequence with no ceiling runs away. A bounded sequence that keeps jumping never chooses a landing place. Completeness supplies a least upper bound for the terms to approach.

exercise.title: Why is a fixed-point equation not a proof of convergence?

statement.p: If a recursive sequence a_{n+1}=F(a_n) converges to L and F is continuous, then L=F(L). In your own words, why can that equation identify a possible limit without proving that the sequence actually converges?

hint.p: A possible landing place is not the same as landing. The recursion a_{n+1}=2-a_n has a fixed point at 1, but the sequence can bounce forever between two other values.

note.p: For a recursive sequence, the equation

statement.p: The next section uses sequences in a new way. Instead of studying a list of terms directly, we build a new sequence by adding the first n terms. If those partial sums settle toward a limit, we will call the result an infinite sum.
